fact: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) is a highly prevalent virus that causes cold sores and genital herpes and increases the chance of contracting human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) by several folds.
Most new cases of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) in Africa occur in people infected with Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV).
The process by which immunity to Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) is generated is incompletely understood.
The first immune cells to become infected by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), Langerhans cells in the epidermis, are not the cells that initiate the immune response.
The dermal dendritic cells thought to be responsible for initiating the immune response to Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) are not likely to be infected.
In human skin models and genital herpes lesion biopsies, an interaction between epidermal Langerhans cells and dermal dendritic cells could relay Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) to the lymph node.

Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) is taken up by epidermal Langerhans cells that then migrate into the dermis, die, and are taken up by another subset of dermal dendritic cells which stimulate HSV-specific T cells in the lymph node.
A mucosal or intradermal vaccine targeting epidermal Langerhans cells and dermal dendritic cells may be required to protect against Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV).
Most neurons have cellular tree-like extensions known as dendrites, which receive input signals from synapses with other cells.
Some neurons have very large and impressive dendritic arbors.
If dendrites were an electrical passive medium, then signals from their periphery could not influence the neuron output activity.
Dendrites are active media that amplify and support pulses called dendritic spikes.
Dendritic spikes are voltage pulses that do not simply add but can also annihilate each other when they collide.
A computational model of excitable dendritic trees was examined to understand the net effect of the complex interactions among dendritic spikes under massive synaptic input.

In contrast to passive trees, excitable dendritic trees have a very large dynamic range, which implies a greater capacity of the neuron to distinguish among the widely different intensities of input which it receives.
The results provide an explanation to the concentration invariance property observed in olfactory processing, due to the very similar response to different inputs.
The modeling approach suggests a microscopic neural basis for the century old psychophysical laws.
The circadian system imposes daily rhythms on behavior, physiology, and metabolism and allows organisms to anticipate daily recurring changes in the environment.
Circadian clocks are composed of clock genes acting in transcription–translation feedback loops.

At the heart of the molecular oscillator are the BMAL1–CLOCK transcription factors that drive expression of Cryptochrome (Cry) and Period genes, which in turn encode inhibitors of BMAL1–CLOCK–driven transcription.
Phosphorylation and other posttranslational modifications specify the activity and stability of clock proteins.
The key mechanism underlying the rhythmic phosphorylation of BMAL1 at Ser90 is mediated by Casein Kinase-2 alpha (CK2α).
CRY proteins facilitate cyclic BMAL1–CK2β binding and subsequent cyclic inactivation of CK2α-mediated BMAL1-S90 phosphorylation in live monitoring of protein–protein interactions.
Lack of cyclic BMAL1–CK2β binding and subsequent cyclic inactivation of CK2α-mediated BMAL1-S90 phosphorylation abolishes circadian rhythmicity.
CRY proteins act as inhibitors of BMAL1–CLOCK transcription and also inhibit BMAL1-S90 phosphorylation in a dual negative-feedback model.
Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is the most severe clinical form of leishmaniasis.

In the Americas, visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is a zoonosis caused by the protozoan parasite Leishmania infantum, an intracellular micro-organism transmitted to humans through the bite of female phlebotomine sand flies.
The domestic dog is considered the main reservoir of Leishmania infantum and human beings are dead-end hosts in visceral leishmaniasis (VL).
Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) occurs in 12 countries of the New World and Brazil accounts for 90% of the reported cases.

The factors associated with infection by Leishmania infantum in visceral leishmaniasis (VL) are only partially understood, making it harder to understand the disease dynamics and the development of effective and well-targeted control measures.
Extracellular vesicle (EV) release has been identified from many organisms in recent pathogen research.
Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are small membrane bound organelles which have different origins, sizes, and composition.
The zoonotic parasite Fasciola hepatica was cultured as a case study to investigate the importance of extracellular vesicle (EV) purification from helminth culture media in this study.
Size exclusion chromatography extracellular vesicle (EV) isolation led to a reduction of contaminating excretory-secretory and tegumental proteins when investigating two purification methods.
Purification methods do not isolate equivalent extracellular vesicle (EV) population profiles with similar EV purities.
Size exclusion chromatography methods are likely better suited for downstream helminth extracellular vesicle (EV) studies and application development compared to a differential centrifugation method.

The damped harmonic oscillator framework has been applied to interrogate numerous engineering systems like the tuned mass damper used in power transmission, automobiles, and buildings to reduce vibrations.
The damped harmonic oscillator framework has been applied to undulatory swimming to understand the emergence of movement due to muscular and/or environmental forcing.

The damped harmonic oscillator framework helps elucidate why flexible bodies can be propelled forward by both internal muscular forcing and external fluid forces as reported earlier in which dead trout were found to swim in the wake of a cylinder.
Forcing triggers the first few deformation modes of the swimmer similar to how appropriate forcing triggers the fundamental deformation modes on a guitar string.
The lower deformation modes produce the best forward propulsion of the body in swimming.
Swimming is viable for small enough frequencies of neuromuscular activation relative to the natural frequencies of the body and for sufficiently stiff elastic properties.
The results identify the key mechanistic parameters that would have been crucial to the evolutionary emergence of swimming animals.
The proposed damped harmonic oscillator framework can help understand neural control of movement in swimming as well as control of underwater vehicles.

The antiproliferative response to anticancer treatment results from concurrent effects in all cell cycle phases, where molecular control pathways called checkpoints are activated and cells may be arrested to repair DNA damage or killed if they are not able to succeed in the repair process.
The complexity and inter-cell variability of the antiproliferative response phenomena are not captured by the available methods, and the origin of the dose-dependence of the response remains elusive.
The experimental-computational method presented in this work discloses and measures the individual responses of cell cycle controls in each phase and generation.

The method exploits jointly data sets obtained by flow cytometry and time-lapse in vivo imaging with a suitable experimental design to achieve a full reconstruction in silico of the actual movement of cell cohorts following X-ray exposure.
The method provides separate and quantitative measures of the dose-dependence of G1, S, and G2M checkpoint activities in subsequent generations.

Best fit parameter values from the method are actual measures of the probability of activation of the specific pathways of arrest, repair, or death within the cell population, linking the molecular scale to the macroscopic response with full appreciation of its dynamics and inter-cell heterogeneity.
Herpesviruses are supremely successful mammalian parasites.
Herpesvirus infections rarely present until well established.
Using Murid Herpesvirus-4, a relative of the Kaposi's Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus, the olfactory neuroepithelium was identified as a major portal of host entry.
Heparan sulfate (HS) binding, which is common to many herpesviruses, played a key role in host entry by Murid Herpesvirus-4.
The heparan sulfate of most epithelia is solely basolateral and therefore inaccessible to incoming, apical virions.
The olfactory neuroepithelium displayed heparan sulfate on its apical surface.
The apical heparan sulfate on the olfactory neuroepithelium comprises a dense meshwork of the neuronal cilia that mediate olfaction.
Incoming virions bound to the neuronal cilia of the olfactory neuroepithelium.
A recombinant form of the virion glycoprotein H/L heterodimer also bound to the neuronal cilia of the olfactory neuroepithelium.
Some virions tracked down the neuronal cilia to infect neurons in the olfactory neuroepithelium.
Other virions were transferred to the microvilli of adjacent sustentacular cells in the olfactory neuroepithelium.

The central role of heparan sulfate in host entry by Murid Herpesvirus-4 and the paucity of accessible heparan sulfate on other epithelia suggest that many heparan sulfate-binding herpesviruses could follow a similar path of host entry.
Genetically identical cells growing in the same environment can vary in their cellular state and behavior.
Such heterogeneity may explain why some cells in an isogenic population can survive sudden severe environmental stress whereas other cells succumb.
Cell-to-cell variation in gene expression has been linked to variable stress survival.
How and why transcript levels vary across the transcriptome in single cells is only beginning to emerge.
Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was used to measure cell-to-cell heterogeneity in the transcriptome of budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).
There are surprising patterns of variation across known sets of transcription factor targets, indicating that cells vary in their transcriptome profile both before and after stress exposure.

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis combined with live-cell imaging of transcription factor activation dynamics revealed some cells in which the stress response was coordinately activated and other cells in which the traditional response was decoupled.

The observation that some cells have a coordinately activated stress response while others have a decoupled traditional response suggests unrecognized regulatory nuances that expand understanding of stress response and survival.
Eukaryotic cell chemotaxis has efficiency, sensitivity, and a huge dynamic range that have proven very hard to explain.
Cells respond to shallow gradients of chemotactic molecules with directed movement, but the mechanisms remain elusive.

Most current models predict that cells have an internal “compass” produced by processing the extracellular signal into an intracellular mechanism that points the cell towards the gradient and steers it in that direction.
The internal compass does not exist; instead, the cell orients itself simply by making use of its pseudopods, which are the dynamic finger-like projections on the surface of the cell.

A computational model of the movement of a cell without a compass shows that the cell moves in a convincingly natural way simply by using its pseudopods, which respond to positive- and negative-feedback loops.
The concentration of the chemoattractant molecule modulates the amount of positive feedback in the pseudopod response.
No signal processing other than modulation of positive feedback by chemoattractant concentration is necessary for the cell movement in the computational model.
The simple computational model reproduces many observations about normal chemotaxis.
The computational model accurately predicts the angle at which new pseudopods split off from old ones, which had not been previously measured.
The computational model demonstrates that pseudopod-based mechanisms are powerful enough to explain chemotaxis.
Much of what is known about genetics has come from studying only a tiny fraction of the genome’s sequence, the part that primarily codes for proteins.
The genome has many other features outside the protein-coding regions, some of which play an important biological role.
Transposable elements, which are repetitive sequences present in many species, make up around half of the mouse genome.
Transposable elements are ‘selfish’ elements because their spread within the genome does not necessarily benefit the host organism.
Sometimes transposable elements can be ‘domesticated’ and used to the host’s advantage.
Transposable elements can generate new genes.
The non-coding sequences of transposable elements can regulate the activity of other nearby genes or even those elsewhere in the genome.
It remains unclear to what extent transposable elements have shaped genome regulation throughout evolution.
One idea is that the spread of transposable elements can help to establish large regulatory networks whereby many genes are collectively regulated to produce a specific output.
It has not been fully explored how effective transposable elements are at regulating gene expression.
Todd et al. investigated whether particular transposable elements that are suspected to boost the activity of other genes are essential for normal gene expression in early mouse development.
Todd et al. genetically edited stem cells from the inner and outer layer of the early mouse embryo to find transposable elements that promote gene expression.
Some transposable elements were found to be important for gene regulation in early mouse development, but not all of the candidates tested were needed to maintain expression levels.
Several transposable elements were turned off simultaneously by compacting specific stretches of DNA so that they could no longer be activated.
When 34 transposable elements were inactivated at once, only three transposable elements had a significant impact on gene expression.
Whether or not a given transposable element regulates gene expression cannot be predicted solely from profiling the structure and sequence of the genome.
It is important to interrogate the effect transposable elements have on a gene's role within a cell.
Transposable elements are largely disregarded in genomics due to technical difficulties in analysing these repetitive stretches of DNA.
Characteristic variations within a population may in part be driven by differences in transposable elements, which may also be implicated in diseases such as cancer.
Identifying which transposable elements are important for driving gene expression and linking their actions to specific traits could aid the discovery of important genetic variants.
The cells of nearly all organisms need iron as this metal plays an important role in a wide range of biological processes.
Iron can trigger the formation of harmful molecules that can damage cells.
The amount of iron in cells is tightly controlled and any extra iron is safely stored away.
Most of the iron in the body is stored within a protein called ferritin.
Ferritin is broken down to release iron as it is needed in a process known as ferritinophagy.
Cells use several systems to break down proteins, one of which is called autophagy and has been linked to ferritinophagy.
During autophagy, a bubble-like structure called an autophagosome engulfs proteins that need to be removed and delivers them to a compartment in the cell where they can be broken down.
In 2014, researchers showed that a protein called NCOA4 on the surface of autophagosomes targets ferritin for destruction.
When iron levels are high in the cell, the amount of NCOA4 on the autophagosomes is low.
Low amounts of NCOA4 on autophagosomes lead to fewer ferritin molecules being broken down.
Low iron levels lead to an increase of NCOA4 on autophagosomes, which promotes ferritinophagy and increases the amount of iron in the cell.
A region of NCOA4 directly interacts with a particular subunit of ferritin and this interaction is necessary to deliver ferritin to autophagosomes.
The amount of NCOA4 varies depending on whether NCOA4 interacts with another protein called HERC2, which targets proteins for destruction by a structure called the proteasome.
HERC2 only binds to NCOA4 when iron levels are high, which leads to NCOA4 being broken down by the proteasome.
When iron levels are low, HERC2 does not interact with NCOA4.
The presence of more NCOA4 leads to more ferritinophagy and increases the amount of iron in the cell.
Red blood cells, which depend highly on iron, do not develop properly in zebrafish that have lower amounts of the NCOA4 protein.
All skilled actions rely on precise connections between the sensory and motor areas of the brain.
Sensory areas receive and analyse input from the senses.
Motor areas plan and trigger muscle contractions.
Precisely adjusting the connections between sensory and motor areas and other brain areas enables humans to learn new skills.
Precisely adjusting the connections between sensory and motor areas and other brain areas helps humans to relearn skills lost as a result of brain injury or stroke.
About 70 years ago, psychologist Donald Hebb proposed that whenever two neurons are active at the same time, the connection between them becomes stronger.
The idea that 'cells that fire together, wire together' became known as Hebb’s rule.
Many studies have shown that Hebb’s rule can explain changes in the strength of connections between pairs of neurons.
New results show that Hebb’s rule can explain how connections between entire brain regions become stronger or weaker.
The data were obtained using a technique called optogenetics, in which viruses are used to introduce genes for light-sensitive proteins into neurons.
Shining light onto the brain activates any cells within that area that contain the light-sensitive proteins introduced by optogenetics.
Yazdan-Shahmorad, Silversmith et al. used optogenetics to activate small regions of either sensory or motor brain tissue in live macaque monkeys.
Activating small regions of either sensory or motor brain tissue in live macaque monkeys strengthened the overall connectivity between the two areas.
The effects of activating small brain regions were more variable at the level of smaller brain regions, with some connections becoming weaker rather than stronger.
Yazdan-Shahmorad, Silversmith et al. show that Hebb’s rule explains most of the observed changes in brain connectivity.
Many neurological and psychiatric disorders stem from abnormal brain connectivity.
Simple forms of brain stimulation are already used to treat certain neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s disease.

Stimulating the brain to induce specific changes in connectivity may ultimately enable leveraging the brain’s natural learning mechanisms to cure neurological and psychiatric conditions instead of just treating them.
Many organisms have evolved internal biological clocks which are synchronized with the rhythm of light and dark.
Plants and animals can predict the onset of dawn and dusk, and schedule biological processes to specific times of the day thanks to the circadian clock.
Each cell possesses its own circadian clock, which is formed of a complex network of genes and proteins that get activated along a 24-hour cycle.
In mammals, synchronization of circadian clocks happens thanks to a structure in the brain.
Few studies exist that focus on measuring the clocks of individual plant cells.
Gould, Domijan et al. monitor the circadian clock of single cells in seedlings of the plant Arabidopsis thaliana across several days and under constant environmental conditions.
Gould, Domijan et al. use time-lapse microscopy and genetic methods to see when and where one of the circadian clock’s core genes is switched on in Arabidopsis thaliana.
At the level of the plant, Arabidopsis thaliana has two waves of clock gene expression in the root, one that goes up and one that goes down the root.
Various parts of the Arabidopsis thaliana plant have slightly different circadian rhythms, for instance, the tip of the root has a faster clock.
Robust circadian clock rhythms are detected in individual cells across the Arabidopsis thaliana plant.
Clocks in neighbouring cells of Arabidopsis thaliana communicate with each other to keep track of time, which might contribute to the robustness of the circadian rhythms.

Mathematical simulations show that when individual circadian clocks interact, they generate patterns of clock activity across the Arabidopsis thaliana plant, which explains the two waves of gene expression in the root.
Plant circadian rhythms control traits that are crucial for agriculture, such as growth, yield, disease resistance and flowering time.
Certain animal species can sense the Earth’s magnetic field for the purposes of navigation.
One technological goal is to genetically engineer specific cells in the brain or elsewhere so their activity can be controlled using an external magnet.
The dream of controlling cell activity using an external magnet has been called magnetogenetics.
Recent reports claimed to have solved both the scientific and technological challenges of magnetogenetics by discovering or engineering protein molecules that are sensitive to magnetic fields.
Markus Meister calculated how strongly the proteins in the recent magnetogenetics reports would link magnetic fields to cellular activity.
The predicted effects of the proteins linking magnetic fields to cellular activity are too weak to account for the reported measurements by between five and ten orders of magnitude.
None of the recent reports have found a solution to magnetogenetics.
All of the proposed proteins in the magnetogenetics reports use iron atoms to couple to the magnetic field.
The proteins proposed for magnetogenetics contain far too few iron atoms to explain the reported magnetic effects.
The magnetism of small clusters of atoms is exceedingly well understood due to technological interest in making tiny magnets for data storage drives inside computers.
If any of the biological reports of magnetogenetics were correct, they would force a revolutionary rethinking of basic physics.
Cells have to be able to reliably destroy or remove molecules from their interior that they no longer need.
Structures called proteasomes play a central part in the process of cutting up and digesting proteins in cells.
Mammals have several different types of proteasomes, each made up of several protein subunits.
When a cell experiences inflammation, some proteasomes change some of their subunits and form an immuno-proteasome.
Immuno-proteasomes tend to break down proteins more quickly than standard proteasomes.
Liepe et al. combined experiments and mathematical modelling to construct a detailed model of proteasome activity.
The model shows that protein transport into and out of the proteasome chamber are the steps that limit how quickly the proteasomes can break down proteins.
Protein transport into and out of the proteasome chamber are largely responsible for the different rates at which standard and immuno-proteasomes process proteins.
Liepe et al. confirmed the existence of regulatory sites within the proteasome and described how these regulatory sites are arranged.
Problems that alter the rate at which proteasomes break down proteins have been linked to tumors and neurological and autoimmune diseases.
Liepe et al.'s model enables the study of how the proteasome's activity is affected by drugs and facilitates investigation of ways to interfere with proteasome activity for therapeutic purposes.
Viruses need to enter their host’s cells in order to replicate their genetic material and produce more copies of the virus.
A protein shell called a capsid protects the virus during the journey into the host cell.

The structure of the capsid presents a mystery regarding how the protein shell can be strong enough to remain intact as it enters a host cell and yet quickly open up to release the viral genome after replication.
Unlike the capsids of many other viruses, the capsids of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) have irregular structures that rapidly fall apart once removed from the virus.
The irregular structure of HIV capsids has thwarted attempts to study intact HIV capsids in order to understand how they work.
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) hijacks a range of molecules produced by the invaded host cell.
Dissecting the effects of molecules produced by the invaded host cell on the HIV capsid is key to understanding how the capsid disassembles.
Márquez et al. have developed a method that can visualize individual HIV capsids and how they disassemble in real time using single-molecule microscopy.
The method developed by Márquez et al. revealed that HIV capsids differ widely in their stability.
The HIV capsid shell remains closed for a variable period of time and then collapses catastrophically as soon as it loses its first subunit.

Using the new technique, Márquez et al. found that a small molecule drug called PF74 causes the HIV capsid to crack open rapidly, but the remaining shell is then stabilized against further disassembly.
The observations by Márquez et al. reconcile seemingly contradictory observations made by different research groups about how the drug PF74 affects the stability of the HIV capsid.

The method developed by Márquez et al. enables researchers to measure how molecules produced by host cells interact with the viral capsid, a structure that is fundamental for the virus to establish an infection.
The method developed by Márquez et al. could be used to test the effects of antiviral drugs that have been designed to target the HIV capsid.
The new technique developed by Márquez et al. has already been instrumental in related research by Mallery et al., which identifies a molecule found in host cells that stabilizes the HIV capsid.
Neurons are cells in the nervous system that relay electrical signals around the brain and body.
An electrical impulse travelling along one neuron reaches a junction called a synapse with a neighboring neuron.
The electrical impulse stimulates small containers known as vesicles from the first neuron to release their contents into the synapse.
The contents released from vesicles travel across the synapse to the neighboring neuron and may generate a new electrical impulse.
The number of vesicles at a synapse that are ready to be released varies from one to ten.
The more vesicles the neuron releases, the more likely the second neuron will produce an electrical signal of its own.
Not all electrical signals reaching a synapse stimulate vesicles to be released and some signals only release a single vesicle.
Some vesicles have a higher likelihood of being released than others, but this eagerness does not always predict how many vesicles an individual synapse will actually discharge.
Vaden et al. used brain tissue from mice to test the idea that the number of vesicles available at the synapse affects how many vesicles are released without altering their eagerness for release.
Activating an enzyme called protein kinase A increased the number of vesicles released from synapses in mice without changing how likely individual vesicles were to be released.
Inhibiting protein kinase A did not change individual vesicle’s eagerness to be released but decreased the number of vesicles that were discharged in mice brain tissue.
Protein kinase A modifies a molecule on the surface of vesicles known as synapsin, which controls the number of vesicles that are available for release.
The number of vesicles released at a synapse is controlled by two independently regulated parameters: the number of vesicles that are available and how eager individual vesicles are to be released.
The ability of neurons to communicate with each other is disrupted in autism spectrum disorders, Alzheimer’s disease, and many other diseases.
Learning how neurons communicate in healthy brains will help us understand what happens in the neurons of individuals with autism spectrum disorders, Alzheimer’s disease, and many other diseases.
Asthma is a chronic disease of the airways that leads to breathing difficulty and sometimes death.
Asthma affects about 235 million people worldwide, especially children.
Scientists still do not know exactly what causes asthma.
Studies in Europe and North America suggest that individuals born or raised in rural areas are less likely to be affected by asthma.
Few studies have examined asthma in African countries, where urbanization is often quickly increasing.
Examining the factors associated with asthma as more people move to cities may provide new clues about how asthma emerges and how to prevent asthma.
Mpairwe et al. conducted a study with over 1,670 schoolchildren in Uganda.
Children born or raised in rural areas in Uganda were least likely to have asthma.
The risk of asthma doubled among children from small towns in Uganda compared to those born or raised in rural areas.
The risk of asthma tripled in children born or who grew up in the city in Uganda compared to those born or raised in rural areas.
Children whose parents had a higher education and socioeconomic status had the highest asthma risk in the study in Uganda.
The study by Mpairwe et al. is the first step towards identifying environmental and lifestyle factors associated with increased asthma risk in Africa.

A protein pore called the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) channel allows chloride ions to move through the membrane of the cells that line the airways and some other parts of the human body.
Mutations in the genes that encode cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) may reduce the number of pores at the cell surface or stop the pores from working properly.

When mutations in the genes that encode cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) reduce the number of pores or stop the pores from working properly, the cells cannot transport enough chloride, which causes the disease cystic fibrosis.
Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) contains two regions that lie inside the cell known as nucleotide binding domains (NBDs).

The nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) of cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) bind to the chemical energy molecule adenosine triphosphate (ATP), and when ATP binds, two nucleotide binding domains associate to form a dimer and the pore in CFTR opens.
The cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) channel can occasionally open in a spontaneous way that does not require adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

It was not clear whether nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) also formed dimers when the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) channel opened spontaneously without adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

Spontaneous opening of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) channel could reflect nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) occasionally forming a dimer without adenosine triphosphate (ATP) binding or it could occur when the pore occasionally opens without the nucleotide binding domains forming a dimer.

Mihályi et al. studied the behaviour of single human cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) channels produced in frog eggs to explore whether opening of the pore always requires nucleotide binding domain (NBD) dimerization.

Mihályi et al. used normal cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) channels and mutant ones that show differences in spontaneous opening to investigate the change in the way nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) interacted when the channels spontaneously opened or closed.

Mihályi et al. found that the nucleotide binding domain (NBD) dimer forms when the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) pore spontaneously opens, demonstrating that this step happens both with and without adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
Nucleotide binding domain (NBD) dimer formation and pore movement are strictly coupled and this is an inbuilt property of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein.

When adenosine triphosphate (ATP) binds to cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), this only changes how stable the open-pore and closed-pore structures of CFTR are but does not alter the fundamental architecture of the channel.

Ivacaftor is a drug that stimulates spontaneous opening of cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) and has recently been approved for clinical use to treat people with mutations in CFTR.

The new findings about nucleotide binding domain (NBD) dimer formation and pore opening in cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) will be useful to help researchers understand how ivacaftor stimulates the CFTR pore to open.
